subject: english
title: Reading comprehension
setup: Economists often warn against judging a policy by its intentions rather than its results. A city that caps rents to help poor tenants may, over time, see landlords stop repairing buildings or convert flats into offices, shrinking the very supply the cap was meant to protect. Yet the opposite mistake is just as common: dismissing a policy because it has side effects, without asking whether the alternative is worse. A careful analyst therefore asks three questions: what happens if we act, what happens if we do not, and who bears the cost in each case. The answer is rarely as neat as either supporters or critics claim.

questions.question: What mistake do economists warn against first?
options: Judging a policy by its intentions instead of its results
questions.explanation: 'warn against judging a policy by its intentions rather than its results'.

questions.question: According to the passage, how might a rent cap backfire?
options: Landlords may stop repairs or convert flats, reducing supply
The city may collect less tax
questions.explanation: Landlords may 'stop repairing buildings or convert flats into offices, shrinking the very supply'.

questions.question: What is 'the opposite mistake'?
options: Rejecting a policy for its side effects without comparing the alternative
questions.explanation: 'dismissing a policy because it has side effects, without asking whether the alternative is worse'.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the analyst's three questions?
options: What happens if we do not act?
Who bears the cost in each case?
questions.explanation: The three questions are about acting, not acting, and who bears the cost.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards policy debates is best described as:
options: Strongly in favour of rent caps
questions.explanation: The author criticises both errors and says the answer 'is rarely as neat as either supporters or critics claim'.

subject: english
title: Reading comprehension
setup: The value of a currency note lies not in the paper but in the shared belief that others will accept it. This belief is fragile in an odd way: it survives ordinary shocks easily, yet it can collapse quickly once people expect others to lose faith. Central banks therefore guard their credibility as carefully as their reserves. A promise to keep prices stable is useful only if people believe it will be kept even when keeping it is painful. Paradoxically, the less a central bank needs to act to prove its resolve, the stronger that resolve appears.

questions.question: According to the passage, where does a currency note's value come from?
options: The gold kept by the government
The shared belief that others will accept it
questions.explanation: 'not in the paper but in the shared belief that others will accept it'.

questions.question: In what way is the belief described as 'fragile in an odd way'?
options: It survives ordinary shocks but can collapse once people expect others to lose faith
It depends only on the paper used
questions.explanation: The next clause explains it: it survives ordinary shocks yet can collapse quickly.

questions.question: Why do central banks guard their credibility?
options: Because their promises work only if people believe them
questions.explanation: 'A promise to keep prices stable is useful only if people believe it will be kept'.

questions.question: The word 'resolve' in the last sentence means:
questions.explanation: 'resolve' here is a noun meaning firm determination.

questions.question: What is the paradox stated in the last sentence?
options: A bank that rarely needs to prove its resolve appears most determined
questions.explanation: 'the less a central bank needs to act to prove its resolve, the stronger that resolve appears'.

subject: english
title: Reading comprehension
setup: Automation is usually discussed as a threat to jobs, but history suggests a more complicated picture. When automatic teller machines spread, many expected bank tellers to vanish. Instead, because each branch became cheaper to run, banks opened more branches, and tellers shifted from counting cash to selling products and solving problems. The lesson is not that technology never destroys work, for it plainly does, but that it changes which tasks are valuable. Workers who can move towards those tasks do well; those who cannot, or who are given no chance to learn, bear the cost of a progress that others enjoy.

questions.question: What did many people expect when ATMs spread?
questions.explanation: 'many expected bank tellers to vanish'.

questions.question: Why did banks open more branches?
options: Each branch became cheaper to run
questions.explanation: 'because each branch became cheaper to run, banks opened more branches'.

questions.question: What does the author say technology mainly changes?
questions.explanation: 'it changes which tasks are valuable'.

questions.question: Which statement would the author most likely agree with?
options: Workers need chances to learn new tasks
questions.explanation: Those 'given no chance to learn' bear the cost, so the author values chances to learn.

questions.question: The phrase 'a progress that others enjoy' suggests that:
options: The benefits of change may not reach those who bear its costs
questions.explanation: Some bear the cost while others enjoy the gains.

subject: english
title: Reading comprehension
setup: A common error in reading statistics is to confuse a rise in reported cases with a rise in actual cases. When a district opens more testing centres, it will almost certainly record more cases of a disease, even if the disease is no more widespread than before. The same trap appears in crime figures, where better reporting can look like rising crime, and in bank fraud, where improved detection can make a careful bank look careless. The careful reader asks not only 'how many?' but also 'how was this counted, and has the method changed?'

questions.question: What error does the passage describe?
options: Confusing a rise in reported cases with a rise in actual cases
questions.explanation: 'confuse a rise in reported cases with a rise in actual cases'.

questions.question: Why might a district with more testing centres record more cases?
options: More cases are found, even if the disease is not more widespread
questions.explanation: 'it will almost certainly record more cases ... even if the disease is no more widespread'.

questions.question: How can improved detection affect a bank?
options: It can make a careful bank look careless
questions.explanation: 'improved detection can make a careful bank look careless'.

questions.question: Which question does the careful reader add to 'how many?'?
options: How was this counted, and has the method changed?
questions.explanation: Stated in the last sentence.

questions.question: The examples of disease, crime and fraud are used to show that:
options: The same counting trap appears in many fields
questions.explanation: 'The same trap appears in crime figures ... and in bank fraud'.

subject: english
title: Reading comprehension
setup: Compound interest is often called the most powerful force in personal finance, yet its power is easy to underestimate because it works slowly at first. In the early years, a savings account seems to grow only by the money put into it; the interest feels trivial. Only after a decade or more does the interest earned each year begin to rival the deposits themselves. This is why those who start saving early, even in small amounts, often end up ahead of those who save larger sums later. The same arithmetic works against borrowers: an unpaid credit card balance grows in exactly the way a patient saver's account does.

questions.question: Why is the power of compound interest easy to underestimate?
options: It is illegal in some places
questions.explanation: 'its power is easy to underestimate because it works slowly at first'.

questions.question: When does the interest earned each year begin to rival the deposits?
questions.explanation: 'Only after a decade or more'.

questions.question: Who often ends up ahead, according to the passage?
options: Those who save larger sums later
Those who start saving early, even in small amounts
questions.explanation: 'those who start saving early, even in small amounts, often end up ahead'.

questions.question: The word 'trivial' in the passage most nearly means:
questions.explanation: The interest 'feels trivial': unimportant, small.

questions.question: What point does the last sentence make?
options: Compounding also makes unpaid debts grow
questions.explanation: 'The same arithmetic works against borrowers'.
